extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers (K-12) learning/showing_descriptive writing; creative writing learners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and classroom worksheets for teaching and practicing the 'show, don't tell' writing technique: using sensory detail, action, dialogue, and strong verbs to create immersive scenes rather than flat narration. Aimed at educators and students across grade levels for use in language-arts classes or creative-writing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'show, don't tell' writing style: let a reader experience descriptive details of the story through sensory details, actions, or the expression of a character’s emotions instead of the author describing the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains purpose: 'take the reader inside the story' and 'show you what is happening through actions and images, rather than simply relying on narration.' Example contrast given: Tell: 'Lily was scared when she saw the thief.' Show: 'Lily’s heart started racing as a masked man caught the corner of her eye.' Use scenes that put the reader into the character’s mindset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use descriptive language that appeals to the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use descriptive language that appeals to readers’ senses, making them feel as if they are a part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack a scene through sensory details so readers can imagine and interact with the world (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste). Example: instead of saying a character is in Paris, show the lighting of the Eiffel Tower. Worksheets and prompts focus on building sensory imagery to immerse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose strong, specific verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong verb is descriptive and specific; it makes writing more immersive while keeping sentences concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance notes that weak verbs hinder evocative storytelling. Exercises encourage replacing weak or generic verbs with more precise, energetic choices to convey movement and tone (improves immersion and conciseness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey emotions indirectly (show through action/physical cues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey emotions indirectly, allowing readers to empathize and connect with characters rather than being told outright what they feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show emotion via physical reactions, behaviors, and context (e.g., racing heart, clenched fists, hesitant speech) so readers infer feelings. The page emphasizes letting readers 'experience the events through their senses and emotions' rather than relying on explicit emotional labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue to reveal character and narrative details
rubrics_metrics.description: Using dialogue is a neutral way to communicate narrative details without relying on boring description and also teaches readers about characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue reveals tone, vocabulary, perspective and can show character traits (e.g., long-winded speech implies education). Encourage using dialogue to demonstrate relationships, background, and plot-relevant facts instead of exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe environment, atmosphere, and mood to transport readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice describing the environment, the atmosphere, and the mood using sensory details and evocative language to transport readers into the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheets prompt students to create mood via setting elements (lighting, weather, sounds, textures) and to use evocative language that makes scenes come alive rather than summarizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build scenes with action and imagery rather than narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on packing scenes through actions and images so readers can experience events, instead of using narrative summary or telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'telling' sentences that summarize events or states. Positive practice: write scenes that unfold via specific actions, imageable moments, and sequence so the reader witnesses events. The worksheets (e.g., 'Show The Scene', 'Watch It Unfold', 'Craft The Scene') guide incremental scene-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt instruction and practice across grade levels and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: The techniques and worksheets are suitable for students across different grade levels and for varied formats (screenplay, novel, short story, sonnet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation for teachers to integrate these exercises into language-arts classes, creative-writing workshops, or individual practice. Promotes scaffolded practice through prompts and exercises to develop descriptive writing, sensory imagery, character development, and emotional expression.
